A USD 1,000,000 mortgage loan fully amortizes over ten years with level annual payments of USD 135,868 (rate 6.0%). Annual principal repayments are:

**Key correction:** Source key (B) said the false statement was ’duration rises to 5.09 at 7%’; duration does fall, but statement D (WAL rises to 6.05) is also false because WAL does not depend on the discount yield, so the original had two defensible answers.

question:
A fixed‑income portfolio manager is conducting a performance analysis on an agency‑MBS and the underlying pool of commercial mortgages. The manager obtains the following information:

The constant prepayment rate (CPR) of the commercial mortgages loan pool: 14.38%

Debt payments per year on the commercial mortgage loans: USD 730,000

Net operating income per year of the commercial mortgage property: USD 1,825,000

The manager uses the following metrics as benchmarks for the commercial mortgage sector analysis:

Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) of a benchmark obligor: 2.5

Single monthly mortality (SMM) rate of a benchmark security: 0.85%

Which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: The prepayments on the commercial mortgage measured by the CPR shows that the reduction in yield on the MBS will likely be lower compared to that on a benchmark security.
options.B: The prepayments on the commercial mortgage measured by the CPR shows that the reduction in yield on the MBS will likely be higher compared to that on a benchmark security.
options.C: The estimated DSCR of the commercial mortgage implies that the mortgage borrower’s ability to repay the mortgage loan is stronger than that of a comparable benchmark obligor.
options.D: The estimated DSCR of the commercial mortgage implies that the mortgage borrower’s ability to repay the mortgage loan is weaker than that of a comparable benchmark obligor.

solution:
**Key correction:** Mock 4 Q45 quoted the benchmark CPR as 9.76%; the correct value is 9.74% (conclusion unchanged).

**Step by step**

1. DSCR = NOI / debt payments = 1,825,000 / 730,000 = 2.50, equal to the benchmark 2.5.
2. Convert the benchmark SMM to CPR: CPR $= 1 - (1 - \text{SMM})^{12} = 1 - (1 - 0.0085)^{12} = 9.74\%$.
3. Pool CPR 14.38% > benchmark 9.74%, so the pool prepays faster.
4. Prepayments at a given price reduce the MBS yield, so faster prepayment means a larger yield reduction than for the benchmark.

question: With respect to prepayment measures, EACH of the following statements is true EXCEPT:

options.A: PSA assumes lower prepayment rates for young mortgage pools
options.B: 100% PSA assumes a CPR of 0.2% for the first month, increasing by 0.2% per month for the next 29 months when it reaches 6% per year, and remains at 6% per year thereafter

2. Other speeds are multiples of this path: 150% PSA rises 0.3% per month, so it reaches 0.3% × 30 = 9% in month 30.

loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
question: A trustee’s analyst is documenting how the collateral interest collected at an interim year end is applied in a three-tranche CLO with an overcollateralization account of the type described in the reading. The deal pays trustee and management fees. Which sequence correctly describes the order of application?

options.A: Senior coupon; mezzanine coupon; fees; equity residual; overcollateralization account
options.B: Fees; senior coupon; mezzanine coupon; overcollateralization account up to its annual cap; equity residual
options.C: Fees; senior and mezzanine coupons pro rata to their par amounts; equity residual; overcollateralization account
options.D: Fees; overcollateralization account up to its annual cap; senior coupon; mezzanine coupon; equity residual

solution:
**Step 1 – Fees come first**

GARP: in addition to the coupons promised to the bonds, there are fees and other costs, “which typically take priority over coupons”.

⇒ Any sequence that pays coupons before fees (A) is out.

**Step 2 – Then the bonds, top down**

The senior coupon is paid in full before the mezzanine receives anything; the two are not paid pro rata.

⇒ C is out.

**Step 3 – Excess spread: account first, equity last**

Only what is left after the coupons is excess spread. Up to the cap $K$ goes to the overcollateralisation account; the equity receives the remainder.

⇒ D is out: the account is funded from excess spread, after the coupons, never ahead of them.

**Interpretation**

The order fees, senior, mezzanine, account, equity is the interim waterfall of Figure 1. It is also why the equity flow is the first casualty when defaults erode loan interest.

**LO:** CR-22 c: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), 22.1 Waterfall; 22.2 Tracking the Interim Cash Flows

loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
question: A risk committee is reviewing the overcollateralization mechanism of the CLO in the reading, in which part of the excess spread and all recoveries on defaulted loans are paid into an overcollateralization account that earns the money market rate. Which of the following statements about this mechanism is correct?

options.A: Recoveries are paid through the waterfall together with loan interest, so in a year with defaults the equity can receive more cash than in a year without defaults.
options.B: The diverted excess spread is hard credit enhancement: like the equity note, it is fully in place when the deal is issued.
options.C: The account is built up early in the deal’s life, when collateral cash flows are strongest; it pays bond interest if loan interest falls short, and any balance is released to the equity only at maturity.
options.D: The account protects the senior bond only: it may not be used to pay the mezzanine coupon, which must be met from loan interest alone.

solution:
**Step 1 – When the account fills**

Soft overcollateralisation builds credit enhancement “at the beginning of the life of the product, when collateral cash flows are strongest”. In Malz’s example it accumulates funds “while cumulative defaults are low”.

**Step 2 – What the account is for, and when it pays out**

GARP: the funds “will be used to pay interest on the bonds if there is not enough interest flowing from the loans”; any remaining funds “will be released to the equity tranche only at maturity”.

⇒ C states both points correctly.

**Interpretation**

Malz admits the mechanism “is not a robust mechanism for protecting the senior bonds”, but unless defaults come very early it has money in it when loan interest starts to fall short.

**LO:** CR-22 c: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), 22.1 Waterfall; 22.2 Tracking the Interim Cash Flows

loText: Calculate and evaluate one or two iterations of interim cashflows in a three-tiered securitization structure.
question: A CLO analyst at a Toronto pension fund is projecting the final-year waterfall of a five-year CLO with the structure of the reading: 100 loans of USD 1 million paying Libor + 350 bps; senior notes USD 85 million at Libor + 50 bps; mezzanine notes USD 10 million at Libor + 500 bps; equity USD 5 million; Libor flat at 5%. Recoveries are 40% and are paid into the overcollateralization account, which earns 5% and held USD 16.385 million at the end of year 4. By the end of year 4, 24 loans have defaulted, and 6 more default in year 5. Surviving loans pay their final interest and redeem at par at the end of year 5. Which of the following is closest to the mezzanine bond’s credit loss at maturity?

options.A: USD 4.12 million
options.B: USD 5.12 million
options.C: USD 5.94 million
options.D: USD 7.52 million

solution:
**Step 1 – Account at maturity**

$16.385 \times1.05 = \text{USD} 17.204$ million

⇒ The year-4 balance earns one more year of interest before it is released.

**Step 2 – Terminal available funds**

Survivors = 100 − 24 − 6 = 70: final interest 70 × 0.085 = 5.950, redemption 70.000, final-year recoveries 0.4 × 6 = 2.400.

$F = 17.204 + 5.950 + 70.000 + 2.400 = \text{USD} 95.554$ million

**Step 3 – Senior test**

Senior due $85 \times1.055 = 89.675 \le F$ : paid in full, leaving 95.554 − 89.675 = 5.879.

**Step 4 – Mezzanine test**

Mezzanine due 10 × 1.10 = 11.000; it receives 5.879.

Credit loss $= 11.000 - 5.879 = \text{USD} 5.12$ million

⇒ The equity receives nothing.

**Interpretation**

With 30 cumulative defaults the mezzanine recovers only USD 5.879 million of the USD 11.0 million it is owed (it loses about 47%), while the senior is untouched: the thin junior tranche absorbs the hit once the equity is gone.

**LO:** CR-22 e: Calculate and evaluate one or two iterations of interim cashflows in a three-tiered securitization structure.

- **Reference:** Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), Tracking the Final-Year Cash Flows, Table 22.2

CR-22 • Structured Credit Risk • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
question:
Concepts • shape B3·S4, D15·S4

A model validation analyst at a Singapore bank is reviewing the note on the correlation parameter of the bank’s tranche pricing model. The model joins the default-time distributions of the 125 CDX.NA.IG constituents with a Gaussian copula and a single constant pairwise correlation, which is recalibrated each day so that modelled standard tranche values match market prices. Which of the following statements in the note is correct?

options.A: The parameter is the constituents’ default correlation, the correlation of their default indicators, so it can be checked against historical joint default frequencies.
options.B: The parameter is a copula correlation inferred from prices; it has no direct economic interpretation, but it equals the correlation of a Gaussian single-factor model.
options.C: The parameter is the constituents’ asset return correlation, so it can be measured directly as the correlation of their equity returns.
options.D: The parameter is a physical (real-world) correlation, because it is estimated from the observed prices of liquid traded tranches.

solution:
**Step 1 – Name the parameter**

A correlation entered in a copula and calibrated to market prices is an **implied credit correlation**: GARP calls it “an estimate of the copula correlation derived from market prices”, not a distinct theoretical concept.

**Step 2 – What a copula correlation is**

Copula correlations are “the values entered into the off-diagonal cells of the correlation matrix” of the copula. They “have no direct economic interpretation”, but “the correlation of a Gaussian copula is identical to the correlation of a Gaussian single-factor factor model”.

⇒ B is correct.

**Interpretation**

Because it is backed out of prices with risk-neutral default probabilities, the parameter is a risk-neutral, market-based number. Like spread correlation it is a market rather than credit risk concept, and it moves every day with the tranche prices.

**LO:** CR-22 l: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), 22.4 Implied Correlation; Summary of Default Correlation Concepts

loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
question:
Correlation

The head of a correlation trading desk explains to a new market risk manager why the desk’s standard CDX tranche positions are risk-managed differently from the bank’s holdings of cash CLO tranches. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: A standard tranche has a partial spread01 to each of the 125 constituents, and moves in spreads or in implied correlation cause mark-to-market changes; in a cash CLO, default rate and correlation changes alter fundamental value.
options.B: A standard tranche is valued with physical default probabilities taken from the constituents’ ratings, so its main sensitivity is a default01, measured by shocking those probabilities by 10 bp.
options.C: Implied correlation is a pure credit-risk parameter that is fixed when a standard tranche is first traded, so it causes no mark-to-market changes in the desk’s positions.
options.D: The CDX spread premium is reset every day to the fair spread of the constituents, so standard tranche positions carry no exposure to changes in constituent spreads.

solution:
**Step 1 – The standard tranche’s sensitivities**

GARP: “The value of each tranche has a distinct risk-neutral partial spread01, rather than a default01, that is, sensitivities to each of the constituents of the IG 125.” Each spread01 is itself a function of the implied correlation, which “varies in its own right”.

⇒ Spreads and implied correlation both move the mark-to-market value.

**Step 2 – The cash CLO**

In the cash CLO, “changes in default rates and correlation result in changes in expected cash flows and credit losses”, that is, changes in fundamental value.

⇒ A is correct: implied credit correlation is as much a market-risk as a credit-risk concept.

**Interpretation**

This is why a correlation desk reports spread01s and correlation sensitivities, while a buy-and-hold CLO investor watches default rates and the waterfall.

**LO:** CR-22 l: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), 22.4 Credit Index Default Swaps and Standard Tranches; Implied Correlation

loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
question:
A structured credit analyst at an Australian superannuation fund monitors the fund’s equity tranche in a CLO with the same structure as the one simulated in the reading. For loans with a one-year default probability of 2.25%, the simulation grid gives (equity value in AUD million; bond writedowns in percent of tranche par):

| Copula correlation $\rho$ | 0.00 | 0.30 | 0.60 | 0.90 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equity value | 4.44 | 4.98 | 5.61 | 6.33 |
| Mezzanine writedown | 0.00 | 7.35 | 12.82 | 15.49 |
| Senior writedown | 0.00 | 0.52 | 2.14 | 5.05 |

The market price of the equity tranche has risen from AUD 4.98 million to AUD 5.61 million, while the risk-neutral default probability implied by the loans’ CDS spreads has stayed at 2.25%. Which of the following statements should the analyst include in the report to the investment committee?

options.A: The implied correlation has fallen from 0.60 to 0.30, because a higher equity price signals that defaults are now expected to be spread more evenly across scenarios.
options.B: The implied correlation has risen from 0.30 to 0.60, and the mezzanine bond’s expected writedown has fallen, because the mezzanine tranche behaves like the equity tranche at any default rate.
options.C: The implied correlation has risen from 0.30 to 0.60, reflecting a higher market assessment of systematic risk, and the senior bond’s expected writedown rises from 0.52% to 2.14% of par.
options.D: The implied correlation has risen from 0.30 to 0.60, and because it is estimated from rating-based physical default probabilities, it is a credit risk rather than a market risk parameter.

solution:
**Step 1 – Back out the implied correlation**

With the CDS-implied default probability fixed at 2.25%, the only free input is the copula correlation. An equity value of 4.98 matches $\rho= 0.30$; a value of 5.61 matches $\rho= 0.60$.

⇒ The market now prices the equity as if defaults were more clustered: implied correlation has risen from 0.30 to 0.60.

**Step 2 – Read the other tranches at the same default probability**

Senior writedown: 0.52% → 2.14% of par (up). Mezzanine writedown: 7.35% → 12.82% (up).

⇒ At this low default rate the mezzanine sits with the senior: higher correlation hurts both bonds while it helps the equity.

**Interpretation**

C is correct. Higher correlation means a low but material probability of a state with unusually many defaults, the systematic risk that reaches the senior bond even on a diversified pool, while the equity, now a “lottery ticket”, gains from the higher chance of a low-default state.

**LO:** CR-22 i: Explain how the default probabilities and default correlations affect the credit risk in a securitization. CR-22 l: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), 22.3 Means of the Distributions, Table 22.3; 22.4 Implied Correlation

loText: Describe the process of valuing a synthetic CDO using the spread payments approach and the Gaussian copula model of time to default approach.
question: A structured credit analyst at a French bank prices the standard iTraxx Europe tranches with the one-factor Gaussian copula, keeping the index spread, recovery rate and hazard rate fixed. She raises the copula correlation from 0.10 to 0.30. Which of the following describes the effect on the tranches?

options.A: All tranche spreads rise, because higher correlation raises each company’s probability of default.
options.B: The equity tranche becomes riskier and the senior tranches safer, because defaults become more frequent in every scenario.
options.C: The equity tranche becomes less risky and the senior tranches riskier, so the equity tranche’s price for protection falls and the senior tranche spreads rise; the index spread is unchanged.
options.D: No tranche price changes, because the expected loss on the whole portfolio does not depend on correlation.

solution:
**Step 1 – What correlation changes**

Each name keeps the same hazard rate, so the portfolio’s expected loss and the index spread are unchanged. Correlation changes how defaults cluster: few defaults and many defaults both become more likely.

**Step 2 – Effect by tranche**

More scenarios with few defaults protect the equity tranche; more scenarios with many defaults reach the senior tranches. With the January 2007 inputs (index 23 bp), the standard market model gives an equity upfront of 13.3% at $\rho= 0.10$ and 5.5% at $\rho= 0.30$, while the 12 to 22% spread rises from about 0 to 5 bp.

⇒ The equity tranche becomes less risky, the senior tranches riskier.

**Interpretation**

This is why tranche quotes carry information about correlation, and why a single implied correlation can be backed out of each tranche price (CR-13 g).

**LO:** CR-13 f: Describe the process of valuing a synthetic CDO using the spread payments approach and the Gaussian copula model of time to default approach. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.25 (GARP CR Ch.13), 13.9 Role of Correlation in a Basket CDS and CDO; Practice Question 13.26

CR-13 • Credit Derivatives • Vardeez: MODERATE

loText: Define the two measures of implied correlation: compound (tranche) correlation and base correlation.
question:
A correlation trader at a London bank reviews GARP’s implied correlations for 5-year iTraxx Europe tranches on 31 January 2007:

| Detachment point | 3% | 6% | 9% | 12% | 22% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Compound correlation | 17.7% | 7.8% | 14.0% | 18.2% | 23.3% |
| Base correlation | 17.7% | 28.4% | 36.5% | 43.2% | 60.5% |

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The base correlations form a smile: they fall from the equity tranche to the 0 to 6% tranche and then rise.
options.B: The 0 to 6% tranche has a base correlation of 7.8%, the lowest in the capital structure.
options.C: The market is pricing every tranche with the one-factor Gaussian copula and a single correlation of about 18%, the equity tranche’s correlation.
options.D: The compound correlations form a smile, lowest for the 3 to 6% tranche, while the base correlations rise steadily with the detachment point; the two coincide at 3%, where the tranche is both a single tranche and a base tranche.

solution:
**Step 1 – Read the compound row**

17.7%, then 7.8% for 3 to 6%, then rising to 23.3%: down then up, a smile with its low point at the mezzanine tranche.

**Step 2 – Read the base row**

17.7%, 28.4%, 36.5%, 43.2%, 60.5%: rising with the detachment point, a skew. At 3% the tranche {0, 3%} is both the first tranche and a base tranche, so both measures are 17.7%.

⇒ D is correct.

**Interpretation**

GARP: the compound correlations exhibit a “correlation smile” and the base correlations a “correlation skew”. Both would be flat if the market priced with the model.

**LO:** CR-13 g: Define the two measures of implied correlation: compound (tranche) correlation and base correlation.

- **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.25 (GARP CR Ch.13), 13.10, Implied Correlation, Table 13.8

loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
question: A UK card issuer that brings a credit card ABS to market several times a year is choosing the legal form of its issuing vehicle. Its US counsel recommends a trust arrangement; its London counsel says a company incorporated in Jersey would serve. Which of the following statements about the two forms is correct?

options.A: A company SPV is the usual form in the US market, because US accounting rules are satisfied by a single entity that issues notes directly against its assets.
options.B: Choosing the trust form removes the need for a true sale, because the trustee then holds the receivables on behalf of the originator.
options.C: A company SPV cannot be bankruptcy remote, so investors in its notes keep a claim on the originator if the receivables underperform.
options.D: In the trust arrangement the receivables are sold to a master trust that deposits them in a grantor trust; the notes rest on a beneficial interest, which further distances the originator.

solution:
**Step 1 – Both forms are SPVs**

GARP: “An SPV is a legal trust or company” that is not linked to the originator and is bankruptcy remote. A company SPV can be bankruptcy remote just as a trust can.

⇒ C fails.

**Step 2 – Where each form is used**

The trust “is more common in the US market, and its interests are represented by a Trustee”; in the Euromarkets SPVs “are often incorporated as companies”. Schweser: the company form may not distance the originator enough for US accounting purposes.

⇒ A swaps the geography.

**Step 3 – What the trust arrangement adds**

The originator sells the receivables to a master trust (SPV 1), which deposits them in a grantor trust (SPV 2) and receives a beneficial interest. The notes are backed by that beneficial claim, which further distances the originator from the assets (Figure 1).

⇒ D is correct. A true sale is still needed (B fails), and the trustee acts for the investors, not the originator.

**Interpretation**

For a card issuer that comes to market several times a year, the trust form also carries the master trust structure, which issues series after series from one pool of receivables.

loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
question: A supervisor asks a risk analyst to compile a list of sound early warning indicators of a potential liquidity problem at the bank. Which of the following sets contains only genuine warning signals?

options.A: Negative publicity concerning an asset class the institution holds; a decline in the share price; widening spreads on the institution's debt and credit default swaps; significant deterioration in the institution's financial condition.
options.B: Negative publicity concerning an asset class the institution holds; a decline in the share price; an increase in credit lines extended to the institution; an increase in the weighted average maturity of liabilities.
options.C: A decline in the share price; widening credit default swap spreads; an increase in credit lines extended to the institution; significant deterioration in the institution's financial condition.
options.D: Widening credit default swap spreads; an increase in credit lines extended to the institution; significant deterioration in financial condition; an increase in the weighted average maturity of liabilities.

solution:
**Concept tested:** Discriminating genuine early warning signals from developments that improve rather than threaten the liquidity position.

Every candidate item in the option set is a real observable. The task is to sort them by direction: does the development make a liquidity problem more likely, or less?

| Observable | Signal | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Negative publicity about an owned asset class | Warning | Counterparties reassess the institution's exposure and may withdraw funding or widen haircuts |
| Share price decline | Warning | A market-based view that the institution's prospects have deteriorated; often precedes funding withdrawal |
| Widening debt and CDS spreads | Warning | The direct market price of the institution's credit; the clearest single signal that funding is repricing |
| Significant deterioration in financial condition | Warning | The fundamental driver behind the market signals |
| Increase in credit lines extended to the institution | Not a warning | More committed funding available is an improvement. It is a drop in credit lines that signals trouble |
| Increase in the weighted average maturity of liabilities | Not a warning | Longer-dated funding reduces rollover risk. It is a shortening of liability maturity that signals trouble |

loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian bank is developing a prepayment model for a new CAD mortgage product that has no prepayment history. The team proposes to use the prepayment history of an older mortgage product as a data proxy.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| New product balance (expected) | CAD 3.4 billion |
| Proxy source | Older fixed-rate product, 2014 to 2025 |
| Main difference | New product allows penalty-free partial prepayment |

Which of the following best describes how the proxy should be treated under best practice for model development?

options.A: The proxy should be carefully identified, justified and documented, and the developers should be able to show it is suitable and consistent with the theory and chosen methodology.
options.B: The proxy may be used without separate documentation, because the documentation standard applies to the model’s theory and methodology rather than to the data used to build it.
options.C: The proxy should not be used, because models for new products may be developed only once representative internal data on the new product have been accumulated.
options.D: The proxy should be identified and justified by the validation function once the model is in use, because the assessment of development data belongs to ongoing monitoring.

solution:
Treasury analyst at a Canadian bank proposing an older mortgage product’s history as a proxy for a new CAD product.

**Concept and theory**

Output quality depends on input quality, so the guidance gives the data used to develop a model “critical importance”. Its requirements build in steps:

1. There should be a rigorous assessment of data quality and relevance, with appropriate documentation.
2. Developers should be able to demonstrate that the data and information are suitable for the model and consistent with the theory behind the approach and with the chosen methodology.
3. If data proxies are used, they should be carefully identified, justified and documented.
4. If data are not representative of the bank’s portfolio, or assumptions are made to adjust them, these factors should be tracked and analysed so that users are aware of potential limitations; this is particularly important for external data and for new products, instruments or activities.

A proxy is a stand-in for data that do not exist. It is legitimate, and often unavoidable for a new product, but it introduces a gap between what the model learned from and what it will be applied to. The requirements above exist to make that gap visible and defensible rather than hidden.

loText: Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.
question: A validator at a Singapore bank is reviewing an SGD mortgage prepayment model. She and the developer hold different views on a key prepayment assumption, and both views are reasonable and equally valid. The developer has noted the assumption’s limitations in the model documentation. Which course of action best reflects the role of MRM in this situation?

options.A: Decide which view of the assumption is correct and require the developer to adopt it, since conceptual questions of this kind are ultimately a matter of right or wrong.
options.B: Ensure transparency, making sure the assumption and its limitations are communicated to users so that they understand when the model can be safely used and when to stop.
options.C: Accept the assumption without further action, since limitations that are discussed in the model documentation can be relied on to be understood by all users.
options.D: Remove the conceptual risk entirely by requiring the developer to recalibrate the model until it is shown to be valid in every possible market environment.

solution:
Validator at a Singapore bank and a developer hold equally reasonable but different views on a prepayment assumption.

**Concept and theory**

GARP distinguishes two sources of model risk. Execution errors are errors in doing what the model is designed to do; they are matters of right or wrong. Conceptual errors arise from wrong assumptions or techniques and are “much more difficult to identify because, unlike execution errors, they may not be a matter of right or wrong. Different reasonable modelers can have different and equally valid opinions on an assumption.”

MRM cannot “correct” such a disagreement by decree. GARP states: “In those situations, the role of model risk management is to ensure transparency.” Understanding the limitations of a model and communicating them clearly to users, who might not be quantitatively savvy, is crucial. Modelers may discuss limitations in the documentation, “but this does not mean that the users of the model will necessarily be aware of them or understand them.” MRM should therefore ensure the assumptions are communicated “in a manner that is useful to their understanding of when the model can be safely used and when its use should be discontinued.” A model can be right in one context and wrong if the context changes.
